In yet another game... well that game is toxic-as-fuck, but I think that's because it's a free to play game modelled to be exactly like the first one. I'd love to see Blizzard start a second WoW dev team and employ some of the people working on the largest WoW private servers, to establish official Vanilla, Burning Crusade and Wrath of the Lich King realms and perform any necessary maintenance and bug fixes.


Jagex pretty much did the same thing with Old School RuneScape when they shut down 2006scape (A private server that attempted to emulate 2006-era Runescape). They took on-board the feedback of how many people hated RuneScape 3 and its various changes, saw that 2006scape was gaining a lot of hype, and gave their fanbase what they wanted.

Fun fact, OSRS is now the *most popular* version of RuneScape, regularly managing more active players at once than RuneScape 3, and that is only set to grow even further when the OSRS dev team plan a phased-release of a brand new content (Zeah) exclusive to OSRS which will increase the size of the game world immensely at the beginning of 2016.

That's right, OSRS is so popular that Jagex are releasing *new* content for that version of the game. While I won't go so far as to say Blizzard need to release new Vanilla/TBC/Wrath content, a launch of legacy servers running on legacy versions of the game client is what Blizzard need to be doing with WoW.

If Blizzard made an old-school WoW client available and allowed subscribers to download the older clients and experience the game as it was originally intended, I would resub in a heartbeat. Hell, even if they did a Jagex and hired a few extra devs to produce new content for the Vanilla game such as the (originally intended) Emerald Dream raid and slew of cut zones and islands in that era, then I can see Legacy realms eclipsing the current release realms with absolute ease.

It's quite sad that you can only experience the previous Azerothian game world, and the original class abilities, talents and itemisation which fuelled the game these days by playing on a private server. Meanwhile on retail, any content outside of Dungeon Finder, Raid Finder and Hellfire Citadel remains abandoned, and cannot be experienced at its originally intended difficulty level even if you could 'level down' your character like in RIFT and Final Fantasy XIV thanks to years and years of immense power creep through really horribly designed game updates.

Blizzard say it's too hard, or 'the technology simply isn't there', but there are people who have reverse-engineered the 1.12, 2.4.3 and 3.5 clients and managed to run a slew of private servers which have both emulated and built upon a Blizz-like experience.

Ahhh, a typical "Just make more money" argument. For a lot of people, this simply isn't an option.

Let's say you work in retail or customer service and earn the minimum wage, which a lot of people do. The average full time contract in Britain is for 37.5 hours per week, and the national minimum wage in the UK is £7.20 (for a worker over 25 years old, whereas it gets even lower for anyone below that age.)

Hence, a 25+ worker can earn £270 per week, £14,040 per year, or £1,170 per month in pre-tax pay.

Now let's subtract taxation and National Insurance contributions from this figure. [Rather than bore you with lots of mathematical calculations, I found a website capable of calculating the income](https://www.incometaxcalculator.org.uk/?ingr=14040&time=1&yr=2017&age=0#). This gives us a net annual wage (rounded to nearest penny) of £12,714.40 per year, £1059.53 per month, £244.51 per week, or £6.52 per hour.



Since UK employees are usually paid at the end of the month, we're now concerned with the net monthly figure of £1,059.53. [Let's subtract the average monthly energy bill on a small house/flat from that figure](https://www.ukpower.co.uk/home_energy/average-energy-bill), which is £61 per month, [then subtract food (£140) and internet (£20) from that monthly bill, on the assumption that the worker is living the austere lifestyle of a student.](http://www.ed.ac.uk/studying/international/finance/cost-of-living)

This means that we now have an income of £838.53 per month after taxation and basic necessities (gas/electricity, groceries/food, internet connection, which is almost mandatory in today's society, and is required to play World of Warcraft, so screw it, we're factoring this in as well.)

Since we're now concerned with the disposable income of a minimum wage 25+ UK worker, let's compare the monthly income of £838.53 per month to [average UK rent prices circa October 2015, according to statistics quoted by the Telegraph from Homelet:](http://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/property/11984097/London-rents-now-a-record-108pc-higher-than-rest-of-UK.html)

* Greater London - There is no way that anybody on a salary that low can live in London with its average rent costs of £1,560 per month. London is just *that* heavily price gouged due to overpopulation, gentrification, and heavy demand for properties. Even most Londoners can barely afford to live in London on their increased average salaries compared to the rest of the UK.

* South East England - Perhaps if you're lucky enough to find a cheap property far away from London to rent, you could maybe live a very austere life in South-East England. Otherwise, good luck, because South East England is populated pretty highly with workers who commute into London on a regular basis.

* South West - At £872 per month, the average property in the South West is pretty unaffordable and will leave you living an incredibly austere lifestyle.

* East Anglia - At £809 per month, we finally have a point where we can calculate the percentage of disposable income that a WoW realm transfer priced at £17 would be: 838.53 - 809 = 29.53, and (17 / 29.53) *100 = ~57.57% of your disposable income.

Holy crap did this game age badly. A few thoughts I have on the game (mostly about the graphics):

* Some of the textures look nice but others look washed out and blurry. The grass textures and skybox in particular look dated in retrospect.

* There are very limited options for increasing the rendering distance of foliage (without mods), meaning that you'll still have instances where grass straight up disappears and becomes a flat texture from a few dozen yards away.

* HDR lighting and anti-aliasing are mutually exclusive. Why?

* No Borderless or Windowed (Fullscreen) option is quite bad for a game from 2006. This was something World of Warcraft had during the Vanilla days and that game came out in 2004. Instead, we only have the choice of Fullscreen or Windowed. Hell, Borderless wasn't even patched in to the game. 

* Why is the 'Ultra High' quality preset on the Options menu set to 1024x768? I get it, HD resolutions and 16:9 aspect ratios weren't much of a thing back then, but this game hardly felt future-proof.

* The user interface is horrible on PC in terms of hotkey setup. When looting bodies for example, there aren't hotkeys for every action you can do, especially no 'Loot all' hotkey. Or if there was a hotkey for that, it sure as hell didn't appear in the Controls menu.

* The water effects look nice, but only from up close. If you're looking at a lake or river from a distance, the reflection will look incredibly pixellated, even on maximum settings.

* Having every town, city and DLC quest location unlocked as a fast travel point from the get-go completely ruins the exploration aspect of the game, especially if you're trying to rush through the story mode.

* Why the fuck am I getting quest notifications about DLC content while I'm in the tutorial level?

* These character models look fugly. There is just something about their shape, textures, and the wrinkles on their face that puts them straight in the uncanny valley. Even Final Fantasy X on the PS2 released back in 2001 had better looking character models with more realistic looking faces than Oblivion.

* The Arena is by far the most fun sidequest in the game. Otherwise - and this will be dependent on the company or campaign you work with - expect the following:

* Low wages. Unless you're working for an insourced customer service department, or are working in a developing country where wages are dirt cheap anyway, don't expect to be paid above the minimum wage, at least when doing gruntwork.

* Having to escalate your call to a supervisor frequently. Sometimes, there is very little you can do to control a call if the person on the other end doesn't like the process - no matter how much you sugar-coat it.

* Favouritism. Some call centres have notoriously bad company cultures surrounding them. Generally, it's the inbound ones that frequently rack up negative reviews on a well-known professional review site that you need to be wary of. In these call centres, don't expect to progress, unless you've made really good friends. By the way, I would suggest avoiding outbound work like the plague unless it involves courtesy-calls and not telemarketing.
